Michchhāmi Dukkaḍaṃ (मिच्छामि दुक्कडम्), also written as michchha mi dukkadam, is an ancient Indian Prakrit language phrase, found in historic Jain texts. Its Sanskrit equivalent is "Mithya me duskrtam" and both literally mean "may all the evil that has been done be in vain".[1]
It is used widely in Jainism for the Pratikramana ritual every nine days and also on the last day of Paryushana called Samvatsari in the Svetambara tradition, and Kshamavani in the Digambara tradition.[2][3] The phrase is alternatively interpreted and said to mean, "May all my improper actions be inconsequential" or "I ask pardon of all living beings, may all of them pardon me, may I have friendship with all beings and enmity with none".[1][2] As a matter of ritual, Jains greet their friends and relatives on this last day with Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ, seeking their forgiveness.
The phrase is also used in Jain monastic practice on a more periodic basis as a part of a monk's or nun's confessional and repentance mantra during the pratikramana (fourth avasyakas) ritual, particularly when they are venerating images or murti of Tirthankaras in Jain temples.[2][4]
The phrase miccha me dukkadam, is an ancient Prakrit language phrase that is commonly found in Jain texts. The Sanskrit version is mithyā me duṣkṛtam. It is related to a section of Jaina monastic code of conduct called the avasyakas (Prakrit: osayas, obligatory observations or duties).[2] It means "may the evil of it be in vain".[3] In the phrase, mithyā refers to 'being fruitless', me means 'my', duṣkṛtam refers to 'bad deeds'.
The Jain scholar Hemachandra gave it a symbolic etymological basis in his Yogasastra verse 3.124, as the following:[3]
- mi is "miu maddava", connoting "gentleness"
- cha is "dosanam chayana", connoting "the veiling of faults"
- mi, me is "a-merae thiya", connoting "abiding in the limitless"
- du is "duganchami appanam", connoting "I loath myself"
- ka is "kadam me pavam", connoting "I have committed sin"
- dam is "devemi tam uvasamenam", connoting "I go beyond it through attaining to calm"
The phrase "tassa micchami dukkadam" has been interpreted in a number of ways, or implied to mean more, from literal to symbolic. Examples include:[2]
- "May that fault have been done in vain [have no effect]"
- "May all my improper actions be inconsequential"
- "My fault has been due to error"
- "May all my transgressions be forgiven"
- "I ask pardon of all living beings, may all of them pardon me, may I have friendship with all beings and enmity with none."
The phrase michchāmi dukkaḍaṃ is found in the Airyapathiki Sutra, verses 3.124 and 3.130 of the Yoga sastra.[3] The verse is a part of the airyapathiki-pratikramana ritual and prelude to the caitya-vandana (worship in a temple). It contains and ends with micchami dukkadam:

SOURCE thejainreligion.in (Micchami Dukkadam Meaning, Messages & Wishes):
In short
"Micchami Dukkadam" is a Prakrit phrase meaning "may my bad deeds be fruitless" — a sincere request for forgiveness. Jains say it to family, friends and even those they have wronged on Samvatsari, the final day of Paryushan, letting go of a full year's ill will before starting fresh.
मिच्छामि दुक्कड़म्
"If I have caused you offense in any way, knowingly or unknowingly, in thought, word, or deed, then I seek your forgiveness."
Micchami means "to be fruitless" (forgiven) and Dukkadam means "bad deeds". Therefore, the phrase translates to: "May my bad deeds (towards you) be fruitless."
It is a concept of washing away the hate and toxic feelings that may have accumulated over the year. On the day of Samvatsari (the final day of Paryushan), Jains say this to friends and foes alike, resetting their social and spiritual karmas.
खामेमि सव्व जीवे, सव्वे जीवा खमंतु मे।
Khamemi Savve Jiva, Savve Jiva Khamantu Me
मित्ती मे सव्व भूएसु, वेरं मज्झं न केणई।
Mitti Me Savva Bhuyesu, Veram Majjham Na Kenai
                        "I grant forgiveness to all living beings,
May all living beings grant me forgiveness.
My friendship is with all living beings,
My enemy is totally non-existent."

Michhami Dukkadam: The Jain Festival That Teaches Us How to Say Sorry, Forgive & Start Fresh
by Pandas Box on Sep 21, 2026
Have you ever had a fight with your brother or sister?
Maybe they took your favourite toy.
Maybe you ate the last piece of chocolate and blamed it on someone else. 😬
Maybe you said something mean when you were angry… and later thought, “Okay. That was not very nice.”
But then came the awkward part.
How do you say sorry?
You want to.
But your ego says, “Why should I say it first?”
Sounds familiar?
There’s a beautiful Jain tradition that speaks directly to this feeling.
It is called Michhami Dukkadam.
But it’s much more than simply saying sorry.
So, what does Michhami Dukkadam actually mean?
You may have heard Jains say “Michhami Dukkadam” during Paryushan as they seek forgiveness for any harm they may have caused, knowingly or unknowingly.
A commonly given explanation of the Prakrit phrase is:
Michhami — may it become fruitless
Dukkadam — the wrong or bad deed
In simple words:
“If I have hurt you, I’m sorry. I hope that wrong doesn’t leave a lasting mark.”
But here’s where it gets really interesting.
They don’t just ask people for forgiveness
The Jain tradition takes the idea much further.
A forgiveness prayer says:
“I forgive all living beings.
May all living beings forgive me.
I have friendship with all living beings.
I have enmity with none.”
All living beings.
Not just Mum.
Not just Dad.
Not just the friend you fought with yesterday.
Everyone.
The idea is to seek forgiveness from the living beings we may have hurt through our thoughts, words or actions.
And that includes lives we might not even notice.
Picture this.
You’re walking through a garden and spot a tiny ant.
You move your foot and keep walking.
No big deal, right?
But what if you had never noticed the ant at all?
Or you pluck a flower without thinking.
Or snap at your friend because you’re having a bad day.
Sometimes we hurt without meaning to.
Sometimes, we don’t even realise we did.
And that’s what makes this idea so beautiful.
It asks us to pause.
To look around.
And wonder:
“Did I hurt someone?”
“Could I have been kinder?”
And then comes the tricky part: forgiveness
Michhami Dukkadam isn’t only about asking others to forgive you.
It is also about forgiving others.
Which, let’s be honest, can be HARD.
“But they started it!”
“They broke my stuff!”
“She said it first!”
“I didn’t even do anything!”
Yep. We’ve all been there 😅
Forgiving someone doesn’t mean saying that what happened was okay.
It simply means choosing not to carry that anger forever.
And maybe that’s why children understand this better than we think.
Two siblings can have a full-blown fight at 4 PM…
…and be sharing a packet of chips at 4:07.
“Fine. I’m not angry anymore.”
Done.
No 17-page internal investigation.
It’s not just a once-a-year “sorry”
The idea of looking back at our actions is connected to Pratikraman, a Jain practice of reflecting on where we may have gone wrong and seeking forgiveness. The annual Samvatsari Pratikraman is an important part of this practice during Paryushan.
So Michhami Dukkadam isn’t just:
“Oops, it’s that day. Send the WhatsApp message.”
It’s about taking a moment to look back.
Maybe you were unkind.
Maybe you lost your temper.
Maybe you hurt someone without meaning to.
And maybe you can make it right.
